title: Every building the public bought, with its earlier sales
question: Before the City bought a building, when had it last changed hands, what value did that sale set on the tax roll, and how far above that was the City’s price?
finding: 41 of the 43 purchases could be matched to a parcel; the rolls from 2007 to 2025 show at least one earlier sale date for 29 and a value re-set by that sale for 22. Among the 8 finished buildings that can be compared like for like, the widest gaps are 888 Post Street ($9,999,000 on the 2020 roll after a sale dated 3 July 2019, $29,000,000 paid 1.9 years later, +190%; work added in between); 3055-3061 16th Street ($1,967,514 on the 2016 roll after a sale dated 13 May 2014, $5,600,000 paid 7.3 years later, +185%; no change shown on the roll); 1000 Sutter Street (Hotel Granada) ($30,074,998 on the 2020 roll after a sale dated 25 July 2019, $46,000,000 paid 1.3 years later, +53%; too soon for the roll to show any change); 681-687 Ellis Street ($14,280,000 on the 2022 roll after a sale dated 14 June 2021, $19,900,000 paid 0.8 years later, +39%; too soon for the roll to show any change). At 888 Post Street the City was already the tenant when it bought (Base Annual Rent $1,500,000, Landlord Work $5,000,000 under file 200043). In 4 purchases the price was below the assessed value the roll carried just before, among them 1660 and 1670 Mission Street ($18,500,000 against $48,512,468). Where a later roll can be checked against a stated price it matches: in 2 of 2 nonprofit purchases the next roll equals the Budget Analyst’s price to the dollar ($46,000,000 and $50,000,000).
how: Purchases and prices are those in the property screens (Board of Supervisors file titles, and the Budget Analyst’s table for two hotels a nonprofit bought with State and City money). For each parcel, every roll year from 2007 to 2025 was read; a sale date is listed if any roll shows it. The value set by a sale is land plus improvements on the first later roll where the land value moves by more than the yearly inflation factor, looked for up to four rolls after the date. Years held run from the prior sale date to the date the City’s file was introduced. Change is the City’s price over that value; change per year divides by years held (at least one). New, renovated or unchanged is read from year built, units, class code and improvement value between the roll after the prior sale and the last roll before the City’s file. Lots that were renumbered are followed through the City’s parcel change log.
limits: The roll records no price. The value that appears after a sale date is an indicator of the price, because California law re-sets assessed value to the price paid when a property changes hands; exemptions, a transfer of part of a property, transfers the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break that link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder would settle what was paid; neither is open data. The roll names no owners, so that the seller to the City is the buyer at the prior sale date is an inference. A higher price a few years on has honest causes: a developer finishing a building, a seller who renovated or emptied it, a market that rose, or a first sale at a distressed price. A hotel bought to be used as housing may also have been sold with furniture, a business or a lease that the land-and-building value leaves out. Sale dates are thin on the 2017 roll and from 2020 on.
